CRITICALITY ANALYSIS OF HTR-10 USING THE HIGH-TEMPERATURE GASCOOLED REACTOR CODE PACKAGE

Anders Jia Yi Choo*, Sicong Xiao *Singapore Nuclear Research and Safety Initiative, National University of Singapore. Singapore, Singapore *anders@nus.edu.sg

## ABSTRACT

The  10  MWt  High-Temperature  Gas-Cooled  Reactor-Test  module  (HTR-10)  is  a  prototype pebble-bed reactor intended to act as a stepping stone for the development of Pebble-Bed Reactor (PBR)  technology  in  China.  The  International  Atomic  Energy  Agency  (IAEA)  released  a  set  of benchmark problems that can serve to assess the accuracy  of existing codes. These benchmarks support the code-to-code validation of computational models and methods for subsequent safety analysis of future pebble-bed reactors. In this work, initial criticality calculations of the HTR-10 were performed using simplified Serpent Monte Carlo models of the reactor configurations, with consideration of both random, discrete pebble distributions in the pebble bed core. A model was also built in parallel using the HTR Code Package (HCP), a highly-integrated coupling backbone that  integrates  multiple  physics  modules,  to  validate  against  the  Serpent  model  of  the  same configuration.  The  simulation  results  demonstrated  that  the  HCP  code  showed  good  agreement with  the  Monte  Carlo  solution  in  terms  of  their  initial  criticality,  which  indicates  HCP’s capabilities to accurately model the HTR-10.

KEYWORDS:  HTR-10;  Pebble-bed  reactor;  Benchmark  analysis;  Initial  criticality;  Serpent; HCP

## 1.  INTRODUCTION

The  pebble-bed  High  Temperature  Gas-cooled  Reactor  (HTGR)  is  a  promising  candidate  for  nextgeneration  nuclear  power  plants  due  to  its  inherent  safety  features  and  high  temperature  capability. The TRISO particles' multi-level barriers, combined with the low power density, result in a significant improvement in safety features, enabling simplified design and reduced costs.

Initiated in 1992, the HTR-10 is a 10 MWt pebble-bed type, graphite-moderated, and helium-cooled modular  HTGR  operated  by  the  Institute  of  Nuclear  Energy  Technology  (INET).  The  reactor  first reached criticality in December 2000 and achieved its full power operation in January 2003. During that period, the HTR-10 was used as a tool for the validation of neutronics, and a set of benchmark specifications  for  its  initial  critical  core  experiment  by  the  IAEA  [1].  Several  studies  have  been conducted on PBRs, including analyses of its thermal-hydraulic behaviour, fuel behaviour, and safety characteristics. Calculations were performed using a diffusion-based system code known as the Very Superior Old Programs (VSOP), specifically developed for reactor physics simulations with pebblebed  reactors  [2].  Jing  et  al.  reported  the  initial  core  configuration  of  the  reactor  and  criticality calculations in 2002 and criticality analyses have been conducted soon after by Colak and Seker [3, 4]. In addition to VSOP, other system codes have been developed for reactor physics simulations with pebble-bed reactors. For instance, the Monte Carlo method has been used  for criticality problems in pebble-bed  assemblies,  including  studies  dealing  with  criticality  analysis  for  the  HTR-PROTEUS experimental facility using MCNP-4A. [5]. The Multi-Group TINTE (MGT) was later developed for time-dependent  reactor  dynamics  to  handle  transients  and  accident  simulations  for  HTGRs  while, VSOP is used mainly for core design and reactor operation on a longer time scale [6]. More recently,

the HCP, developed at the Jülich Research Center (FZJ) and RWTH Aachen, facilitates the coupling of these physics modules in a highly integrated manner, allowing for more user-friendly simulation of steady-state and transient operating conditions for pebble-bed reactors [7].

As part one of the coordinated research programmes, IAEA conducts scientific research and analytical evaluations of benchmark problems. In this study, preliminary validation of the HCP is performed by conducting criticality analyses based on transport calculations and comparing the results to the same HTR-10 model built in the Serpent, a Monte Carlo code [8]. These efforts ultimately allow for more accurate safety assessments.

## 2.   DESCRIPTION FOR FIRST CRITCALITY

### 2.1. Model Description

The HTR-10 reactor has a core vessel that has a cylindrical shape with a cone structure and discharge tube  at  the  bottom.  Like  any  PBR,  the  core  is  filled  with  pebbles,  consisting  of  fuel  pebbles  and ‘dummy’ pebbles – spheres the same size as fuel pebbles but made only of graphite. The fuel pebbles are  billiard-ball-size  spheres  containing  TRISO-coated  fuel  particles  embedded  in  a  matrix.  The TRISO  particles  enclose  the  UO2  fuel  instead  of  it  being  uniformly  distributed,  creating  a  double heterogeneity  within  the  pebble-bed  reactor.  During  the  operation  of  the  reactor,  the  pebbles  are loaded  at  the  top  and  gradually  move  downwards  through  the  core  area.  The  core  of  the  HTR-10 reactor is composed of a cylindrical cavity above a conical zone, known as the "conus”, which directs the pebbles towards a discharge tube. The core, conus, and discharge tube are surrounded by blocks of graphite, known as the reflector, and boronated carbon blocks that have holes for coolant flow, control rods, shutdown absorber balls, and other uses [9].

In the initial criticality configuration, the voids in the core and reflector were filled with ambient air, instead of the helium that is used to cool the reactor during operation. The conus and discharge tube were filled  with  "dummy"  pebbles  while the  cylindrical  core  was  initially  loaded  with  a  mixture  of 16,890  fuel  pebbles  and  dummy  pebbles  in  a  ratio  of  57:43  until  the  core  became  critical.  The volumetric packing density of the entire core was assumed to be 0.61,  which is the widely accepted average  value  based  on  empirical  data.  Based  on  the  pebble  diameter,  the  core  diameter,  and  the assumed packing fraction, it can be confirmed that the number of pebbles used in the initial critical experiment  is  equivalent  to  a  level  core  height  of  123.06  cm.  The  reflector  region  is  composed  of numerous graphite blocks that are surrounded by boronated carbon bricks at the periphery. Prior to the first criticality experiment, both the reflector and pre-loaded graphite pebbles were dehumidified [9]. For simplicity, the water content is excluded from the reflectors in the calculations.

A fuel  pebble is composed of two distinct regions: an outer graphite shell and an inner fuel region. The fuel region contains coated fuel particles that are embedded in a graphite matrix. The fuel particle consists of multiple layers, with the fissile material UO2 forming the core of the particle. Surrounding the core is a porous carbon buffer layer, followed by a dense inner pyrolytic carbon layer providing a diffusion  barrier  for  fission  products,  a  layer  of  silicon  carbide  supplying  strength,  and  finally,  an outer pyrolytic carbon layer protecting the SiC layer and impeding diffusion [9]. The nominal data for the fuel and dummy pebble materials, including the coated fuel particles, are listed in Table 1. These parameters  and  specifications  will  be  used  as  preliminary  benchmarks  in  Serpent  and  HCP  for  the HTR-10 initial criticality analysis.

### 2.2. Benchmark Problems Specifications

The benchmark  model used for the critical configuration of HTR-10 is the simplified model, where the  upper  layer  of  the  core  is  approximated  as  a  flat  plane  and  the  reflectors  are  made  azimuthally symmetric.  Furthermore,  the  coolant  flow,  control  rods  and  small  absorber  balls  (KLAK)  channels that are present in the high-fidelity model are azimuthally homogenised and replaced with structural materials.  The  total  number  of  fuel  and  dummy  pebbles  remains  unchanged  at  9627  and  7263, respectively,  with  each  pebble  containing  8335  coated  fuel  particles.  The  simplified  model  makes certain  adjustments  to  accommodate  the  limitations  of  codes  that  have  less  sophisticated  geometric modelling capabilities. In the benchmark configurations used in this study, the region between the top reflector  and  top  of  the  pebble  bed  core  was  filled  with  a  void  space,  in  contrast  to  the  IAEA document's benchmark configuration, where this region is filled with either helium or air [1].

The  original  B1  benchmark  problem  involves  determining  the  amount  of  loading  for  the  first criticality  with  the  core  filled  with  helium  and  core  temperature  of  27  ℃,  without  the  insertion  of control rods or shutdown absorbers [1]. The initial criticality experiment reported a loading height of 123.06 cm from the upper surface of the conus region and thus, this height is used for both the Serpent and  HCP  model.  The  core  temperature  refers  to  the  temperature  of  the  fuel  pebbles  and  the

surrounding reflectors encompassed within the core physics model, as described in the HTR-10 core configuration.

The original  B2  benchmark  problem  involves  calculating  the  effective  multiplication  factor  (keff)  of the full core at three different core temperatures: 27 °C (known as B21), 120 °C (known as B22) and 250 °C (known as B23), without the insertion of control rods or shutdown absorbers [1]. This problem is  designed  to  investigate  the  temperature  dependence  of  keff.  This  benchmark  employs  the  same model as the B1 benchmark, but with a taller pebble height of 180.12 cm for the full-core analysis, in contrast to the 123.06 cm height used for the initial core criticality analysis. Due to the taller pebble bed height of 180.12 cm used for full-core criticality analysis in the B2 benchmark, the total number of pebbles increases to 24721, achieving a packing fraction of 0.61. This total consists of 14091 fuel pebbles and 10630 dummy pebbles, where each fuel pebble still contains 8,335 coated fuel particles.

The original benchmark was established prior to achieving the actual first core criticality, and it has been  modified  to  reflect  the  actual  experimental  configuration,  thus  creating  a  revised  version  also known as the deviated benchmark [1]. The core temperature reported was 15 °C and the critical core height remained at 123.06 cm. Compared to the original benchmark specifications, the changes made in the deviated benchmark is as follows:

(a)  The density of the dummy pebbles increased from 1.73 g/cm

## 3.  MODELLING METHODOLOGY

The  complex  geometry  in  pebble  bed  reactors  due  to  the  randomly  distributed  spherical  fuel  and dummy  elements,  makes  neutron  transport  in  the  system  difficult  to  accurately  model.  Discrete Element  Method  (DEM)  is  a  computational  technique  that  allows  the  modelling  of  the  packing structure  and  interactions  between  individual  pebbles,  which  explicitly  captures  the  double heterogeneity  of  the  system.  The  positions  of  the  pebbles  are  first  determined  using  a  DEM  code called  LAMMPS  and  these  discrete  coordinates,  together  with  the  radius  and  pebble  type,  are  then used to construct the MC model with Serpent [10]. The model boundaries are modelled in LAMMPS according to the cylindrical core specifications and the pebble bed is generated by randomly pouring the pebbles into the model under the influence of gravitational force and contact forces.  The pebble distribution  evolves  according  to  the  Newton’s  second  law  which  is  defined  through  a  series  of dimensionless  parameters  such  as  friction  coefficient and  normal  elastic constant.  After  the  pebbles have settled, the critical height and number ratio of fuel and dummy pebbles were achieved using a simple post-processing Python script, while ensuring  a packing fraction of 0.61 for the critical core configuration. On the other hand, the random positions of TRISO particles in the graphite matrix of a fuel  pebble  are  generated  with  Serpent’s  particle  automated  disperser  routine,  which  produces  a distribution file that can be used as an input card.  Figure 1 shows the  packed  pebble bed generated with  LAMMPS,  together  with  its  radial  distribution  function.  In  this  case,  the  radial  distribution function, g(r) shows how the density varies as a function of the pair separation distance to a particular pebble. The graph in Figure 1 (b) recorded a peak at a distance 6 cm, which is due the surrounding pebbles in direct contact.

The present study involved performing neutronics calculations using the 3D continuous-energy Monte Carlo reactor physics code Serpent 2, developed at VTT Technical Research Centre [8]. Serpent was selected for this study because it  provides the functionality to create  an explicit stochastic geometry model  that  enables  the  TRISO  particles  and  fuel  pebbles  to  be  defined  explicitly  in  stochastic configurations. The explicit geometry model works on multiple levels, including the particles within a pebble  and  the  pebbles  within  the  core,  as  depicted  in  Figure  2.  This  model  has  been  verified  in realistic double heterogeneous reactor setups. Moreover, it uses delta-tracking methods to simulate the transport  of  neutrons  which  significantly  improve  the  computational  performance  in  geometries. These reasons make Serpent an excellent choice to model double heterogeneous geometries, such as the HTR-10 reactor, with increased accuracy. All the simulations in Serpent were performed using the ENDF/B-VII.0 cross section data library, which is consistent with the library used in HCP [11].

The geometry and material compositions of the simplified HTR-10 benchmark model were based on a technical  document  provided  by  the  IAEA  [9].  The  geometric  cells  provided  in  the  document  are given  in  Figure  3  (a).  In  the  initial  criticality  model,  the  core  was  filled  with  a  pebble  mixture generated with LAMMPS while the lower conus and discharge tube region were filled with dummy pebbles  arranged  in  a  Body-Centred  Cubic  lattice.  The  lattice  in  the  conus  region  was  adjusted  to achieved a packing fraction of approximately 0.61. The region between the top reflector and top of the pebble bed core was filled with a void space, which is consistent with the model built in HCP, while the spaces between the pebbles were filled with either air or helium. The reflector region of the model consists of multiple graphite blocks, which are enclosed by boronated carbon bricks around the edges. The axial cross section of the model and the radial cross section at the height of 300 cm from the top is shown in Figure 3 (b).

An exact replica of the model  built in Serpent  was created in HCP, utilising the TRISHA spectrum code solver and the Bende’s Dancoff factor method [7]. TRISHA utilises a new data library generator, which  helps  the  user  generate  nuclear  cross  section  data  with  full  control.  Unit  cells  used  for  the TRISO  particles  and  fuel  pebbles  are  automatically  updated  to  account  for  the  spatial  and  time dependent nuclide concentrations, which eliminates the need to manually define different unit cells as input [12]. It combines a 0D diffusion solver and a 0D transport code based on the B1 method [13]. An analytical method to calculate the Dancoff factor that is incorporated in the code uses first-flight escape and transmission probabilities while the other method is based on the chord method [14, 15]. Both  methods  have  been  validated  with  Monte  Carlo  calculations  and  are  effective  in  handling  the double heterogeneity associated with pebble bed reactors [7].

The  MGT-3D  code  was  responsible  in  handling  HTGR  transient  and  accident  simulations,  and integrating  it  into  HCP  involves  decoupling  the  MGT  Fluid  Dynamics  (MGT-FD)  and  MGT Neutronics  (MGT-N)  modules  [6].  With  the  MGT-N  module  re-implemented  into  the  HCP framework, calculations of the spatial neutron flux and fission power distribution becomes possible. The  MGT-N  code  employs  a  finite-difference  and  leakage  iteration  method,  and  is  capable  of modelling  steady-state  and  transient  behaviour  of  a  3D  reactor  system  represented  in  cylindrical

coordinates  [16].  All  the  modules  in  HCP  are  linked  by  a  newly  developed  backbone  that  enables integrated and optimised management of the code system’s inputs and outputs [7]. In this work, three input files that deals with different aspects of the simulation in HCP are created to model the HTR-10 based on the benchmark problems. ## 4.  RESULTS

A comparison of the calculated keff using Serpent and HCP for both original and deviated benchmark of the HTR-10 simplified model is presented in Table 2; Serpent was used as the reference solution. The  neutron  population  in  Serpent  was  defined  to  be  5000  neutrons  per  cycle  and  the  statistical uncertainty gave a range of ±0.00080 to ±0.00089.

The relative differences between the calculated keff values obtained from Serpent and HCP falls below 400  pcm  for  both  the  B1  and  B2  benchmark  problem.  Therefore,  this  indicates  a  good  agreement between the two codes and more importantly, the results demonstrate the accuracy of the HCP code in modelling the HTR-10 configuration.

Although both the Monte Carlo and deterministic codes showed good consistency, a possible reason for  the  difference  between  the  calculated  keff  values  could  be  the  hexagonal  regular  lattice  pebble distribution  in  the  conus  region  of  the  Serpent  model,  which  does  not  result  in  an  exact  packing fraction  of  0.61  defined  in  HCP.  In  addition,  the  discrepancies  in  the  initial  criticality  observed between the experimental and computational models could be attributed to uncertainties in the water content of the graphite core.

HCP has been implemented with the aim of achieving a well-balanced trade-off between accuracy and computational burden while ensuring user-friendliness by making use of XML files for the user input. HCP  demonstrates  significant  advantages  over  Serpent  when  considering  the  same  benchmark problem.  On  the  same  machine,  HCP  requires  3  times  less  memory  and  runs  80  times  faster  than Serpent. It is important to acknowledge that a direct comparison between a Monte Carlo code and a deterministic one may not be entirely fair, particularly in the absence of uncertainty analyses for the deterministic code. Nonetheless, HCP offers superior computational efficiency and faster simulations. However, HCP does have certain limitations when it comes to modelling high fidelity systems, such as  accurately  representing  the  azimuthal  configuration  of  control  rod  borings  and  coolant  flow regions.

## 5.  CONCLUSION

A  simplified  HTR-10  model  was  built  using  the  same  input  configuration  as  for  the  first  criticality calculation  using  Serpent  and  HCP  code.  The  Serpent  model  incorporated  a  stochastic  discrete arrangement of TRISO particles within the fuel pebbles and a random distribution of pebbles within the core of the pebble bed using DEM code LAMMPS.

The  comparison  of  keff  values  between  the  simplified  models  of  Serpent  and  HCP  for  the  initial critical core configuration shows an outstanding agreement, indicating the accuracy of the HCP code. This  study  suggests  that  HCP  is  a  reliable  tool  for  modelling  high-temperature gas-cooled  reactors, such  as the  HTR-10.  It  could  be  used  in  future studies  to investigate  other reactor  designs,  such  as HTR-PM or operating conditions. Lastly, the study of neutron spectra and spatial power distributions in future analysis will provide a more comprehensive evaluation of the performance of both Serpent 2 and HCP.
